text: The man at the door was a researcher from the Kanghan Institute, which studied cases the office couldn't classify. The alert had gone out ten seconds ago. He was already here.
Chae asked for four minutes. For what? A third registration category.
The form only had two boxes, but the law behind it had three. The third category dated back to a law from 1995, and nobody had used it in twenty years.
It was called Arrival. Taeo asked what that meant.
He started answering for Nib, saying he came through a seam of light. Chae stopped him. Arrival didn't define what Nib was. She wanted Nib to answer for himself.
The law only said an arrival was someone who came here. It never said from where. Nib decided. File me as an arrival.
Chae pressed Enter.
Taeo asked what she had just done. Nib now had thirty days of protection from seizure, until a review decided his status.
Nib said he already knew what he was. Chae said she knew too. But three reviewers still had to agree.
Her supervisor would ask why she did it. Her answer? Because I can read.
She explained the stakes. If they filed Nib as a construct, he would be Taeo's property, and property can be sold. Taeo had never owned anything anyone wanted.
The review would want evidence, so Chae set up a test with sensors. Nib told Taeo to go first. Of course.
She told Taeo not to give Nib orders. Taeo said he didn't give orders. Nib reminded him. You said stay.
Chae told Taeo to breathe and notice what he felt.
Then Taeo felt it. A pressure in his right palm, like someone else's touch.
Both sensors had changed at the same moment. Nib asked if that connection could take him home. Chae said it was a thread between the two of them. They hadn't found a door home.
Next, Taeo faced the shelves, so he couldn't see, while Nib pressed a foam pad. Nib said he looked like he was being punished.
Now, Taeo said. He felt it. Then again. Two for two. Taeo was never two for two.
Nib asked for once more.
This time Taeo felt nothing. Chae told Nib not to press harder. Taeo admitted he wanted the connection back.
Nib said the obvious. So you can't send me home. Chae admitted they hadn't found a way.
Taeo asked what could help them find Nib's home. His watch post, Nib said.
So Nib drew it. A wall here. A tree behind the wall. From his post, he could see the lower path, and the white bit. The wall was chest high.
Chae searched the public gate surveys. Six recordings matched: a wall, a tree, and high ground.
She warned them that these recordings showed gates, not necessarily Nib's home. But they were the only recordings they had.
Taeo hoped the first one would show Nib's wall.
It didn't. That's not my post, Nib said. Five recordings left. Chae would send all six to Taeo.
In her report she wrote: intermittent sensory response. Sometimes Taeo feels what Nib touches. Taeo asked if that was good. It's true, she said.
As they left, she tried to warn him about whatever the Kanghan researcher would offer. But her supervisor was calling.
In the lobby, the researcher was waiting. Doctor Pyo. Mister Yoon, he said. And you must be Nib.
He handed Taeo a coffee and apologised that it had gone cold. He had been early. Nib wanted no coffee.
Pyo asked Nib if he could ask him one thing. No, said Nib. Wonderful, said Pyo.
Then he made his offer. Kanghan wanted Nib to live with them, under an exclusive observation contract. For fifty million won. About thirty-six thousand dollars.
We'd look after Nib very well, he promised.
Taeo had twenty-four thousand eight hundred won in his account. He did the maths before he could stop himself.
Pyo said he could say no, of course. Take your time, Mister Yoon.
On the way out, Nib asked how much fifty million was. Taeo told him. About five thousand of my lunches.
